Yesterday, reports indicated that Apple once considered creating a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but ultimately decided to abandon the idea.

Bloomberg noted three reasons behind Apple's decision, one of which was not wanting to conflict with the stance Steve Jobs took when unveiling the original iPhone. However, that is almost certainly not the decisive factor...

On the surface, a shorter Apple Pencil that works with the iPhone Ultra does seem like an appealing idea. The device is essentially an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same functionality would clearly make a lot of sense.

Samsung, when it launched the Galaxy Note phablet in 2011, shipped it with an S-Pen stylus. The idea then was that the device could to some extent replace a paper notepad, and that design lasted for a decade with a loyal following, before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman listed three reasons Apple ultimately abandoned the idea:

  • The device would become hard to hold, because the stylus would be mounted on the side of the body rather than the top
  • It would conflict with Jobs's view that a stylus is a poor substitute for a finger
  • It would leave unsightly marks on the screen

I don't see the first point as a major consideration, since mounting the stylus on the top of the device would also be a viable option. Although that would require a very short design, I think it could still work well enough.

The second point doesn't convince me either. Jobs's objection was not to the idea of a smartphone being usable with a stylus, but to existing models at the time having to rely on a stylus to operate. Designing the iPhone so that it could be operated smoothly with a finger was the real breakthrough.

In any case, Jobs also flatly refused to use a touchscreen on the Mac on the grounds of poor ergonomics, yet we still expect upcoming MacBook Pro models to add touchscreens, so Apple is not afraid to overturn the positions once held by its co-founder.

I believe it is the third factor that truly killed the idea. The surface of a folding screen is inevitably far thinner and more pliable than that of existing devices. Apple, as reported, waited a long time before releasing its first folding iPhone precisely because of concerns about the screen's appearance and durability; if an Apple Pencil were allowed to keep rubbing against the screen, both would be affected.

If Apple can resolve this issue in the future, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini to go with a future iPhone Ultra? Let us know in the comments.
